lessons.title: Understanding Box Dimensions and Bee Space
lessons.body:
A deep brood box is the heart of your hive. In Africa, where we often use Langstroth hives, the standard deep box holds 10 frames. Its outside dimensions are 50.5 cm long, 41.5 cm wide, and 24.5 cm deep. But you can adjust slightly to fit your local timber. The critical measurement is the inside width: 37.5 cm. This allows 10 frames with a 9.5 mm bee space between them. Bee space is the gap bees leave openâbetween 6 mm and 9 mm. If the gap is smaller, bees glue it shut with propolis. If larger, they build comb in it. So you must build precisely.

Use a tape measure and a carpenterâs square. Mark all cuts clearly. For the sides (long walls), cut two boards 50.5 cm long, 24.5 cm wide, and 2 cm thick. For the ends (short walls), cut two boards 41.5 cm long, 24.5 cm wide, and 2 cm thick. These are the outer dimensions. The inside length will be 46.5 cm, and inside width 37.5 cm. Check that your frames fit snugly but not tight. A good test: place a frame inside; it should slide down with a light push and hang straight.

In hot African climates, you might reduce the depth to 22 cm to save timber and reduce weight, but keep the inside width for 10 frames. If you use 8-frame boxes, adjust width to 30 cm inside. Always use dry, seasoned timber like cypress, pine, or eucalyptus to avoid warping. Warped boxes break bee space and invite pests. Measure twice, cut once. A small error here means bees build burr comb and you lose honey harvest.

lessons.title: Cutting Box Sides, Ends, and Rabbet Joints
lessons.body:
Now you have your dimensions. You need to cut the boards. Use a circular saw or hand saw. For accuracy, clamp a straight edge as a guide. Cut two side boards: 50.5 cm long, 24.5 cm wide. Cut two end boards: 41.5 cm long, 24.5 cm wide. All boards should be 2 cm thick. After cutting, sand the edges lightly to remove splinters.

Next, cut rabbet joints on the ends of the side boards. A rabbet is a step cut into the edge. This gives a strong, interlocking corner. On each end of the side boards, cut a rabbet 2 cm deep and 2 cm wide (the thickness of the end board). So the side board becomes 48.5 cm long in the center, with a 2 cm step at each end. Use a router or a dado blade on a table saw. If you only have hand tools, use a hand saw and chisel: mark the rabbet, saw down 2 cm, then chisel out the waste. Take your timeâthis joint must be square.

The end boards will fit into these rabbets. Test the fit: the end board should sit flush with the outside of the side board, creating a strong corner. No gaps. If gaps exist, bees will fill them with propolis, making inspections hard. In Africa, where humidity can swell wood, a tight rabbet is better than a loose one. Pre-drill nail holes to avoid splitting. You will need 8 nails per corner: 4 through the rabbet into the end, and 4 toenailed from the end into the side. Use 6 cm galvanized nails. Galvanized resists rust in damp conditions.

lessons.title: Assembling Boxes with Nails, Screws, and Glue
lessons.body:
Assembly is where your box becomes strong. Start with wood glue. Apply a generous bead of waterproof wood glue (like Titebond III or local cassava starch glue) to all rabbet surfaces. Glue alone is strong, but with nails it becomes permanent. Place one side board flat on your workbench, rabbet facing up. Insert an end board into the rabbet. Check squareness using a carpenterâs square. If not square, adjust before nailing.

Nail through the side board into the end board: use four 6 cm galvanized nails, spaced evenly. Then nail from the end board into the side board (toenailing) with two 5 cm nails. Repeat for all four corners. For extra strength, drive one 6 cm screw at each corner, countersunk. Screws hold better than nails in softwood. In Africa, where termites are a threat, use treated timber or add a borate treatment after assembly.

After assembling the box, check for gaps. If any, fill with wood filler or a mix of sawdust and glue. Wipe off excess glue immediately with a damp cloth. Let the box dry for 24 hours. Then sand all outside surfaces smooth. The box should be perfectly rectangular. Measure diagonals: they must be equal. If not, gently push the box into square and add a temporary brace until dry. A well-assembled box lasts 10 years or more. A poorly assembled one warps in one season and lets in rain and pests.

lessons.title: Installing Frame Rests and Handholds
lessons.body:
Frame rests are ledges inside the box that hold the frames. Without them, frames fall to the bottom. Cut two frame rest strips from 2 cm thick timber. Each strip should be 46.5 cm long (the inside length of the box) and 2 cm wide. Nail or screw these strips to the inside of the side boards, flush with the top edge. They must be exactly 1.5 cm down from the top. This creates a 1.5 cm deep recess for the frame ears. The bee space above the frames will be 9 mm when the top cover is on. Use 4 cm nails or 4 cm screws, pre-drilled.

Handholds make lifting the box easy. Cut two handhold cleats from 2 cm thick timber: each 10 cm long and 4 cm wide. Attach one to each end board (the short sides) on the outside. Position them 5 cm down from the top edge, centered. Use two 5 cm screws per cleat, countersunk. Alternatively, you can cut handhold recesses into the end boards using a chisel, but cleats are faster and stronger.

In Africa, where hives are often moved at night to follow nectar flows, handholds are critical. Make sure they are smoothâno splinters. Sand them well. Also, check that frame rests are level. Place a straight edge across them; it should touch both rests evenly. If not, adjust. A 2 mm difference will cause frames to tilt and bees to build cross comb. After installing, vacuum or brush out all sawdust. Bees hate dust and will abscond if the box is dirty.

lessons.title: Building and Attaching Bottom and Top Cleats
lessons.body:
The bottom cleats support the floor and keep the box off the ground. Cut two cleats from 2 cm thick timber: each 50.5 cm long and 4 cm wide. These will run along the bottom of the side boards. Attach them flush with the bottom edge, using 5 cm screws every 15 cm. The cleats create a 4 cm gap under the box for ventilation and to prevent rot. In Africa, where ants are a problem, you can rest the cleats on a stand with oil moats. Do not nail through the bottom of the boxâthe cleats are on the outside.

Top cleats are for the top cover, but you also need a top rim on the brood box. Cut two rim strips: 50.5 cm long and 2 cm wide, and two more 41.5 cm long and 2 cm wide. Nail these to the top edges of the side and end boards, flush with the outside. This creates a lip that holds the top cover in place and prevents rain from blowing in. Use 4 cm nails, pre-drilled. The rim should be level all around.

After attaching, check that the bottom is flat. Place the box on a flat surface; it should not rock. If it rocks, sand the cleats until stable. For the bottom board, you can use a solid piece of 2 cm plywood or tongue-and-groove boards. Attach it to the bottom cleats with screws, but leave a 2 mm gap at the front for drainage. In humid regions, drill a 1 cm hole in one corner of the bottom board and cover with wire mesh to let moisture out. This prevents mold, which kills bee brood.

lessons.title: Finishing and Painting Brood Boxes
lessons.body:
Finishing protects your box from rain, sun, and pests. First, sand all surfaces: outside and inside. Use 120-grit sandpaper, then 220-grit. Wipe with a damp cloth to raise the grain, then sand again. The inside does not need paint, but it must be smooth. Bees will propolize rough spots, making inspections difficult.

Paint the outside only. Use a good quality exterior latex or oil-based paint. In Africa, oil-based paint lasts longer in intense sun. Apply two coats, letting the first dry for 24 hours. Paint the bottom edges and cleats wellâthis is where rot starts. Do not paint the inside or the frame rests. Paint fumes can harm bees. Let the box air out for at least a week before installing bees. If you use treated timber, you may not need paint, but paint still helps reflect heat.

For extra protection, you can dip the bottom 5 cm of the box in melted beeswax or paraffin wax. This seals the end grain. In hot climates, light colors like white or light blue reflect sunlight and keep the hive cooler. Dark colors absorb heat and can cause comb to melt. After painting, check for drips and smooth them. Reattach any hardware. Your brood box is now ready. A well-finished box will last many years, giving you strong colonies and good honey harvests.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Constructing Deep Brood Boxes (Hive Bodies)

In African beekeeping enterprises, the deep brood box â often called the hive body or brood chamber â is the engine room of your honey and colony multiplication business. It houses the queen, brood nest, and the frames that produce replacement bees and surplus honey. A poorly built brood box warps, gaps, and invites pests; a well-built one lasts a decade and protects your investment. This Practical Reference gives you the dimensions, cut lists, assembly methods, and finishing steps used by commercial beekeepers across Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda, Ethiopia, Nigeria, and South Africa, adapted for locally available timber such as cypress, mvule, mahogany, eucalyptus, and treated pine.

Business framing: A single deep brood box typically sells for KES 1,800â3,500 (USD 14â27) in East Africa, or KES 3,500â6,000 with frames and foundation. Building your own cuts your cost per box by 40â60%, which directly increases margin per hive sold and reduces your breakeven point on colony sales. Treat every box as a product, not a project.

1. Understanding Box Dimensions and Bee Space

The Langstroth deep box is the global standard because its dimensions match the bees' natural "bee space" of 6â9 mm (Â¼ââ in). Any gap smaller than 6 mm gets propolised; any gap larger than 9 mm gets filled with comb. Your job as a builder is to hold that tolerance on every cut.

Table 1: Standard Deep Brood Box Cut List (10-frame Langstroth)
Part Quantity Length (mm) Width/Height (mm) Thickness (mm)
Long side (with rabbet)250524119â22
Short end241324119â22
Top cleat (handhold bar)25053019â22
Bottom cleat25054019â22
Rabbet cut (frame rest)â50510 deep Ã 19 highâ

Source: FAO, Beekeeping in Africa (Bulletin 68); KALRO Beekeeping Technical Handbook; and the Langstroth patent specification (1852) as adapted for tropical hardwoods.

Africa note: In humid coastal zones (Mombasa, Dar es Salaam, Lagos, Accra), add 1â2 mm to internal dimensions to allow for timber swelling during the long rains. In semi-arid zones (Machakos, Dodoma, Kano), the same timber will shrink, so cut to exact standard and seal all end grain.

2. Cutting Box Sides, Ends, and Rabbet Joints

Cut all timber to length first, then run the rabbet on the long sides. The rabbet is a 10 mm deep Ã 19 mm high step that forms the frame rest and creates the top edge where the next box or cover sits. Use a table saw with a dado stack, a router with a rabbeting bit, or a hand plane and chisel if power tools are unavailable.

  • Set the saw blade to 10 mm depth and 19 mm width.
  • Run both long sides through the cutter with the inside face down.
  • Check the rabbet with a 19 mm offcut â it should slide in snugly.
  • Cut a 10 mm Ã 25 mm handhold notch in the centre of each long side, 40 mm from the top edge.
  • Sand all cut faces to 120 grit before assembly.

3. Assembling Boxes with Nails, Screws, and Glue

Glue is your structural partner; nails and screws are clamps that hold the joint until the glue cures. Use exterior-grade wood glue (waterproof PVA or polyurethane) because African hives face rain, humidity, and heat cycling.

Table 2: Fastener and Glue Schedule per Brood Box
Joint Fastener Quantity Notes
Side to end (corner)Galvanised ring-shank nails 65 mm6 per corner (24 total)Pre-drill to avoid splitting hardwood
Side to end (reinforcement)Galvanised screws 50 mm2 per corner (8 total)Countersink heads
Cleats to sidesGalvanised nails 50 mm4 per cleat (16 total)Glue both faces
All jointsWaterproof PVA / polyurethane glueâFull coverage, wipe squeeze-out

Source: Based on specifications in FAO Beekeeping in Africa and the Ontario Ministry of Agriculture beekeeping guidelines, adapted to African timber species.

4. Installing Frame Rests and Handholds

The rabbet you cut in step 2 is the frame rest. It must be perfectly level along both sides so frames hang vertically and bee space stays uniform. After assembly, run a straightedge across both rabbets; if a frame rocks, plane the high spots. Handholds are cut or routed into the centre of each long side â 10 mm deep, 25 mm wide, 100 mm long â so two people can lift a full box (25â35 kg) safely.

5. Building and Attaching Bottom and Top Cleats

Bottom cleats (40 mm Ã 505 mm) raise the box off the bottom board and create the correct 9 mm bottom bee space. Top cleats (30 mm Ã 505 mm) reinforce the rabbet and give the cover a landing surface. Attach both with glue plus nails, flush with the outside faces.

6. Finishing and Painting Brood Boxes

Paint only the outside of the box. Never paint the inside â bees will propolise it, and fumes harm the colony. Use two coats of exterior water-based acrylic or oil-based enamel. In coastal Africa, use marine-grade paint or add a copper naphthenate treatment to the bottom 50 mm to resist termites and rot.

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING â Read Before Cutting or Treating Timber

  • Power tools: Always wear safety glasses, ear protection, and a dust mask when cutting, routing, or sanding. Hardwood dust (mvule, mahogany, eucalyptus) is a respiratory hazard and can cause skin sensitisation.
  • Timber treatment chemicals: Copper naphthenate, creosote, and many wood preservatives are toxic to bees. Never treat the inside of a brood box, and allow treated timber to cure for at least 14 days in open air before introducing bees.
  • Lifting: A full deep brood box weighs 25â35 kg. Use two people or a hive trolley. Never lift by the handhold alone when the box is full â the cleat can pull out if under-nailed.
  • Fire: If you use a blowtorch or heat gun to scorch timber, keep a fire extinguisher or water bucket within reach and work outdoors, away from dry grass.
  • Children and bystanders: Keep them at least 5 metres from cutting and treating areas. Store all chemicals in locked cabinets.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Timber selected: Dry, straight-grained, termite-resistant species (cypress, mvule, mahogany, treated pine). Moisture content below 15%.
  2. Cut list verified: 2 sides Ã 505 mm, 2 ends Ã 413 mm, 2 top cleats, 2 bottom cleats, all at 241 mm height.
  3. Rabbet cut: 10 mm deep Ã 19 mm high on both long sides, level along the full length.
  4. Handholds routed: 10 Ã 25 Ã 100 mm centred on each long side.
  5. Glue applied: Waterproof PVA or polyurethane on every joint face before fastening.
  6. Fasteners driven: 24 ring-shank nails + 8 screws per box, galvanised, pre-drilled on hardwood.
  7. Square checked: Diagonals equal within 2 mm; frames hang without rocking.
  8. Painted and cured: Two exterior coats on outside only; 14-day cure before bees introduced.

Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  • FAO â Beekeeping in Africa (Agricultural Services Bulletin 68)
  • KALRO â Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organisation, Beekeeping Resources
  • Ontario Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Rural Affairs â Beekeeping Guidelines (hive equipment dimensions)
  • USDA Agricultural Research Service â Bee Research Laboratory publications
  • Apimondia â International Federation of Beekeepers' Associations (open technical resources)

Business takeaway: Build in batches of 10â20 boxes. Buy timber by the cubic metre, not by the piece. Standardise your cut list and jigs so every box is identical â identical boxes stack, interchange, and sell faster. A beekeeper who can build 20 brood boxes a month at 50% below market price controls both the equipment and colony sides of the value chain.

quiz.q: What is the standard outside length of a 10-frame deep brood box?
quiz.explanation: The outside length of a standard 10-frame deep brood box is 50.5 cm.

quiz.q: What is the correct bee space range?
quiz.explanation: Bee space is the gap bees leave open, typically between 6 mm and 9 mm.

quiz.q: Why is bee space important in hive construction?
options: A) To allow bees to pass
B) To prevent propolis and burr comb
C) To make the hive lighter
quiz.explanation: Correct bee space prevents bees from gluing gaps shut with propolis or building comb in unwanted spaces.

quiz.q: What is the inside width of a 10-frame deep brood box?
quiz.explanation: The inside width is 37.5 cm to accommodate 10 frames with proper bee space.

quiz.q: Which timber is recommended for brood boxes in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Dry seasoned timber like cypress, pine, or eucalyptus resists warping and lasts longer.

quiz.q: What is a rabbet joint?
options: B) A step cut into the edge of a board
C) A glue made from cassava
quiz.explanation: A rabbet is a step cut into the edge of a board to create an interlocking corner.

quiz.q: How deep should a rabbet be cut on the side boards?
quiz.explanation: The rabbet should be 2 cm deep to match the thickness of the end board.

quiz.q: What is the best way to ensure a square box during assembly?
quiz.explanation: A carpenter's square helps check that corners are exactly 90 degrees.

quiz.q: Why should you pre-drill nail holes?
options: A) To make nails go in faster
B) To avoid splitting the wood
D) To make the box lighter
quiz.explanation: Pre-drilling prevents the wood from splitting, especially near edges.

quiz.q: What type of nails are best for beehive construction in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Galvanized nails resist rust in damp conditions, making them ideal for hives.

quiz.q: Why is wood glue used in box assembly?
options: A) To make the box heavier
B) To strengthen joints and seal gaps
quiz.explanation: Wood glue strengthens joints and seals gaps, preventing moisture and pests.

quiz.q: What should you do immediately after applying glue during assembly?
options: A) Let it dry for a day
B) Wipe off excess with a damp cloth
quiz.explanation: Wiping off excess glue immediately prevents it from hardening and making a mess.

quiz.q: How long should you let the assembled box dry before sanding?
quiz.explanation: The glue needs 24 hours to cure fully before sanding.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of frame rests?
options: B) To hold the top cover
quiz.explanation: Frame rests are ledges inside the box that support the frames.

quiz.q: How far down from the top edge should frame rests be installed?
quiz.explanation: Frame rests are installed 1.5 cm down from the top to create the correct bee space.

quiz.q: What is the recommended length for handhold cleats?
quiz.explanation: Handhold cleats are typically 10 cm long and 4 cm wide.

quiz.q: Why are handholds important in African beekeeping?
options: A) They make the hive look nice
B) They help move hives at night
quiz.explanation: Handholds allow beekeepers to lift and move hives, often done at night to follow nectar flows.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of bottom cleats?
options: A) To support the floor and keep the box off the ground
C) To attach the top cover
quiz.explanation: Bottom cleats support the floor and create a gap for ventilation and rot prevention.

quiz.q: How long should bottom cleats be?
quiz.explanation: Bottom cleats run along the side boards, so they are 50.5 cm long.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of top rim strips on a brood box?
options: A) To hold the top cover and prevent rain entry
quiz.explanation: Top rim strips create a lip that holds the top cover and keeps rain out.

quiz.q: Why should you leave a small gap in the bottom board?
quiz.explanation: A small gap allows moisture to drain, preventing mold and rot.

quiz.q: What should you do if the assembled box rocks on a flat surface?
options: B) Sand the cleats until stable
quiz.explanation: Sanding the cleats ensures the box sits flat and stable.

quiz.q: Which part of the brood box should be painted?
quiz.explanation: Only the outside should be painted; painting the inside can harm bees with fumes.

quiz.q: Why is light-colored paint recommended for hives in Africa?
options: B) It reflects sunlight and keeps the hive cooler
quiz.explanation: Light colors reflect heat, preventing comb from melting in hot climates.

quiz.q: How many coats of paint are recommended?
quiz.explanation: Two coats provide good protection, with the first drying before the second.

quiz.q: Why should you let a painted box air out before installing bees?
quiz.explanation: Paint fumes can harm bees, so the box must air out for at least a week.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of dipping the bottom of the box in wax?
options: A) It seals the end grain and prevents rot
B) It makes the box heavier
D) It makes the box waterproof inside
quiz.explanation: Wax seals the end grain, protecting against moisture and rot.

quiz.q: What should you use to fill gaps in the assembled box?
options: B) Wood filler or sawdust and glue
quiz.explanation: Wood filler or a mix of sawdust and glue effectively fills gaps.

quiz.q: How can you check if the box is square after assembly?
quiz.explanation: Measuring diagonals: if equal, the box is square.

quiz.q: Why is it important to sand the inside of the brood box?
options: A) To make it look nice
B) To prevent bees from propolizing rough spots
C) To make it easier to paint
quiz.explanation: Smooth inside surfaces reduce propolis buildup, making inspections easier.
